intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives a way to remember it or warns about a common slip. The section pages gather ideas, terms and a worked example. Work the examples in pencil first, then answer the recall questions without looking.

sections.title: What inclusive education means
sections.big_idea: Inclusive education means **the school changes** so that every child can take part, and the child is never asked to change first.
in_plain_words: General Comment 4 defines inclusive education as systemic reform of content, teaching methods, structures and strategies. It separates four situations that programme documents often blur: exclusion, segregation, integration and inclusion. The test is who adjusts. In integration the child fits the school. In inclusion the school changes.

The idea has a short legal history. Salamanca in 1994 made the regular school the starting point. The CRPD in 2006 turned that into treaty duties in Article 24, and General Comment 4 in 2016 explained them: accommodation is owed immediately, and two parallel systems cannot be sustained. SDG target 4.5 asks for the result to be measured.

diagram.caption: from a conference statement to a measurable target

key_terms.meaning: The CRPD Committee's authoritative reading of Article 24.
Placing a child in a mainstream school on the understanding that she adjusts to it.
An adjustment for one child, owed now and not tied to a diagnosis.
Moving as fast and effectively as possible towards Article 24.
The 2030 target for equal access, with parity indices.

worked_example.title: Name the situation
worked_example.setup: Four children, four school situations. Use the Committee's four words.
steps: A child with cerebral palsy in a hill village has never been enrolled anywhere: exclusion.
A blind child lives and studies in a residential school in the district town: segregation.
A deaf child sits at the back of Class 4 with no interpreter: integration.
The same child has an ISL interpreter, captioned videos and a teacher who plans for her: inclusion.
worked_example.answer: Exclusion, segregation, integration, inclusion. Only the last asks the school to change.

mistakes: Calling any mainstream placement inclusion. Without structural change the Committee counts it as integration.
Reading the definition as a duty on the child or the parent. The duty sits with the system.
Treating General Comment 4 as a text only about disability. Its logic fits any child the system leaves behind.

recall.q: Which paragraph of General Comment 4 defines inclusive education?
recall.a: Paragraph 11.

recall.q: Who holds the right to inclusive education, according to paragraph 10(a)?
recall.a: The individual learner. For a child, the rights of the child outrank a parent's wish.

recall.q: What separates integration from inclusion?
recall.a: In integration the child adjusts to the school's standard requirements. In inclusion the school reforms content, methods and structures.

recall.q: How does paragraph 31 treat reasonable accommodation?
recall.a: As an immediate duty. Denying it is discrimination, and it does not wait for progressive realisation.

sections.title: Models of disability
sections.big_idea: The model you hold decides what you try to fix: **the child, or the barrier**.
in_plain_words: A model of disability is a working answer to where the problem sits. The charity model sees misfortune and answers with kindness. The medical model sees a defect and answers with diagnosis. The social model sees barriers in design, attitude and policy. The rights model adds a duty bearer, a standard and a remedy.

Indian systems carry all four. Disability certificates come from the medical model, many special schools from charity, and the RPwD Act from the rights model. The words matter too: a term decides who is counted. Follow the statute in documents, and ask families which words they use in the classroom.

key_terms.meaning: People are disabled by barriers in the environment, attitudes and institutions.
The child holds rights and the state bears enforceable duties.
WHO's classification that treats disability as interaction between functioning and environment.
A certified disability of at least 40% under section 2(r).
Children with special needs, the term used in Samagra Shiksha and UDISE+.

worked_example.title: Sort the proposals
worked_example.setup: A district plan lists three items. Which model does each reflect?
steps: Item one funds identification camps and certificates: the medical model.
Item two builds ramps and buys large-print books: the social model.
Item three sets up a grievance process for refused admissions: the rights model.
The quick test: money for labelling children, or money for the classroom they will sit in?
worked_example.answer: A mixed plan is normal. A good one spends more on the classroom than on the label.

mistakes: Taking a plan that funds only camps and certificates as inclusion work.
Using a term from one law across another. Follow the statute you are applying.
Forgetting that a child below 40% falls outside entitlements that need a benchmark disability.

recall.q: Where does the social model place the problem?
recall.a: In barriers of design, attitude and policy.

recall.q: Which section of the RPwD Act defines a person with disability?
recall.a: Section 2(s).

recall.q: What is a benchmark disability?
recall.a: One certified at not less than 40% of a specified disability, under section 2(r).

recall.q: Why did statisticians move to functional questions?
recall.a: Asking whether anyone is disabled gets low, unreliable answers. Asking about difficulty seeing, hearing or walking is more consistent across countries.

sections.title: Who is left out in South Asia
sections.big_idea: Exclusion has many routes, so **name the route** before choosing the remedy.
in_plain_words: Wealth, disability, caste and tribe, gender, religion, migration and language all push children out or hold them back inside the classroom. Net secondary attendance rises with wealth in all four countries, and disabled children are counted far less often than they are left out.

Census 2011 found 27% of disabled children aged 5 to 19 had never attended. NSS 2018 found 62.9% of disabled people aged 3 to 35 had ever enrolled in an ordinary school. NEP 2020 shows disabled children falling from 1.1% of primary enrolment to 0.25% at higher secondary. Fees, distance, language, safety and documents each need a different response.

children.label: Language
items: Taught in a language not spoken at home

key_terms.meaning: Share of children of the right age who attend that level.
One fifth of households ranked by wealth.
Children never enrolled or enrolled once and gone.
One group's rate divided by another's, such as poorest to richest.
The home language, the first language of instruction.

worked_example.title: Two readings of the data
worked_example.setup: Use the numbers on the slides.
steps: Pakistan's richest fifth attend secondary school at 65.9% and the poorest fifth at 14.6%.
65.9 ÷ 14.6 = 4.5, so the richest attend at about four and a half times the rate.
Census 2011, disabled children aged 5 to 19: 61% attending, 12% attended earlier, 27% never attended.
61 + 12 + 27 = 100, so the three groups cover every child.
worked_example.answer: A ratio of 4.5 in Pakistan, and three groups that sum to 100. The 12% who left are the first group to look for.

mistakes: Reading a small gap between disabled boys and girls as evidence of equality. The larger gaps lie between kinds of disability.
Quoting 2016-17 NEP figures as current levels. Check the latest UDISE+ tables.
Counting enrolment as inclusion for a child who cannot follow the teacher's language.

recall.q: In which country is the wealth slope in secondary attendance steepest?
recall.a: Pakistan, where the richest fifth attend at about four and a half times the rate of the poorest.

recall.q: What share of disabled children aged 5 to 19 never attended school in Census 2011?
What did NSS 2018 find about special schools?
recall.a: Only 4.1% of those outside ordinary school had ever enrolled in one, so special schools reach very few children.

recall.q: What does the UNESCO GEM paper recommend on language?
recall.a: At least six years of mother tongue instruction, plus teachers trained to teach in two languages.

sections.title: The Constitution and the RTE Act 2009
sections.big_idea: The RTE Act gives every child aged 6 to 14 **a right to a neighbourhood school**, and it points to a repealed disability law.
in_plain_words: Article 21A made free and compulsory education a fundamental right in 2002. The RTE Act 2009 gave it content from 1 April 2010 for Classes 1 to 8. Section 3 grants the neighbourhood school, section 13 bars screening and capitation fees, and section 21 creates School Management Committees with parents.

Section 12(1)(c) reserves at least 25% of entry seats in private schools for disadvantaged and weaker-section children, and disabled children count as disadvantaged. Section 3(3) still refers to the 1995 Act, so read it with section 31 of the RPwD Act. The courts have also set the reach of the Act, and the minority school question is pending.

nodes.label: Notify
nodes.sub: state sets income limit and groups

diagram.caption: the section 12(1)(c) quota, step by step

key_terms.meaning: The fundamental right to free education for ages six to fourteen.
Reserves at least 25% of class I entry seats in private schools.
A child whose family income is below the state's limit.
The school near the child's home.
Option for multiple or severe disability under the s3(3) proviso.

worked_example.title: Seats in the quota
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a private school has 40 seats in its entry class.
steps: The quota is at least 25% of the strength of the class.
40 × 0.25 = 10, so at least 10 seats go to disadvantaged and weaker-section children.
A disabled child is within section 2(d), so she can apply for one of those seats.
Section 13 bars screening. A test at the gate for her application is not allowed.
worked_example.answer: At least 10 of the 40 seats. Admission is the start; the experience inside is a separate question.

mistakes: Treating the seat count under 12(1)(c) as a measure of inclusion. It counts admissions and says nothing about experience.
Citing section 3(3) alone. It points to the repealed 1995 Act.
Assuming the Act reaches minority-run schools. The 2014 ruling placed them outside it, and a reference is pending.

recall.q: From which date was the RTE Act in force?
recall.a: 1 April 2010.

recall.q: What classes does elementary education cover under section 2(f)?
recall.a: Class 1 to Class 8.

recall.q: What does section 13 bar?
recall.a: Screening procedures and capitation fees.

recall.q: Which 2014 case upheld Article 21A and Article 15(5)?
recall.a: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v Union of India, a Constitution Bench.

recall.q: Which provision of the RPwD Act overrides the RTE Act for benchmark disabilities?
recall.a: Section 31(1).

sections.title: The RPwD Act 2016
sections.big_idea: The RPwD Act turns the CRPD into Indian law, and its education duties split between **every child** and **children with a certificate**.
in_plain_words: The Act gives effect to the CRPD and replaced the 1995 Act. Section 2(m) defines inclusive education, and section 2(y) defines reasonable accommodation, limited by a disproportionate or undue burden. Chapter III, sections 16 to 18, covers all children with disabilities, with or without a certificate.

Sections 31 and 32 apply only to benchmark disabilities: free education from six to eighteen and at least 5% of higher education seats. Section 16 lists eight duties, section 17 tells government how to build the system, and the Schedule widens the list to include learning disabilities and autism. The Supreme Court supervises special educator posts.

diagram.root: Education duties in the RPwD Act

key_terms.meaning: Defines inclusive education: students learn together and teaching is adapted.
Defines reasonable accommodation, without disproportionate or undue burden.
A five-yearly survey of school-going children with disabilities.
The list of specified disabilities, grouped into five families and an open clause.
The Supreme Court case on special educator posts.

worked_example.title: Which section applies?
worked_example.setup: Two children. Apply the 40% rule and the chapter split.
steps: Child A has a certified 50% locomotor disability. She is a benchmark case, so sections 31 and 32 apply as well as 16 to 18.
Child B has dyslexia and no certificate. Sections 16 to 18 still apply to her, so her school owes her accommodation and early detection.
Free education to age 18 for child A: 18 − 6 = 12 years of entitlement from the starting age of six.
Child B cannot claim section 31, but the school's section 16 duties are unchanged.
worked_example.answer: Both children are covered by sections 16 to 18. Only child A, with a benchmark disability, also receives sections 31 and 32.

mistakes: Telling a family their child has no rights without a certificate. Sections 16 to 18 apply to all.
Reading 'shall endeavour' in section 16 as a request. Clause (vii) makes tracking each child a duty.
Quoting section 31's choice of school as proof the CRPD Committee approves it. Paragraph 40 points the other way.

recall.q: What is the threshold for a benchmark disability?
recall.a: Not less than 40%, under section 2(r).

recall.q: Which section requires a survey of school-going children every five years?
recall.a: Section 17(a).

recall.q: What minimum share of higher education seats does section 32 reserve?
recall.a: At least 5% in government and aided institutions.

recall.q: Which court case keeps special educator posts under supervision?
recall.a: Rajneesh Kumar Pandey v Union of India, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 132 of 2016.

recall.q: What does section 17(i) allow in examinations?
recall.a: Extra time, a scribe or amanuensis, and exemption from second and third language courses.

sections.title: NEP 2020 and Samagra Shiksha
sections.big_idea: NEP 2020 names the groups, and **Samagra Shiksha pays** for much of the response.
in_plain_words: Chapter 6 of NEP 2020 groups the children the system has left behind as socio-economically disadvantaged groups, or SEDGs: gender, socio-cultural, geographical, disability and socio-economic identities. It proposes inclusion funds, Special Education Zones, boarding and girls' schools, and sets a highest-priority aim for children with disabilities.

Samagra Shiksha, launched in 2018, merged three schemes into one running from pre-school to Class 12. Inclusive Education is one of fifteen interventions. It pays stipends for girls with special needs, identification camps, resource centres and special educators. The approved period ended on 31 March 2026 and states are approving the next phase.

key_terms.meaning: Socio-economically disadvantaged groups, the umbrella term in paragraph 6.2.
A region with large SEDG populations that gets maximum effort.
The proposed National Assessment Centre.
The central scheme merging SSA, RMSA and teacher education.
An annual block-level camp costing Rs 10,000 under the scheme.

worked_example.title: What a stipend adds up to
worked_example.setup: Samagra Shiksha pays a girl with special needs Rs 200 per month for 10 months.
steps: Monthly stipend: Rs 200.
Months paid in a year: 10.
200 × 10 = 2,000 rupees a year for one girl.
The slide reports 3.52 lakh girls supported in 2020-21, so the programme reaches many children with a small amount each.
worked_example.answer: Rs 2,000 a year per girl. Ask where this line sits in your state's budget.

mistakes: Treating every SEDG paragraph as funded. Read which group each paragraph actually pays for.
Quoting the 2021-26 figures as the current phase. The period ended on 31 March 2026.
Treating home-based education as a safe default. NEP 6.12 asks for an audit of it.

recall.q: Which paragraph of NEP 2020 lists the SEDG categories?
recall.a: Paragraph 6.2.

recall.q: When was Samagra Shiksha launched and which schemes did it merge?
recall.a: In 2018, merging Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan and Teacher Education.

recall.q: How many interventions does Samagra Shiksha have?
recall.a: Fifteen, one of them Inclusive Education.

recall.q: What does NEP paragraph 6.12 say about choice?
recall.a: Children with benchmark disabilities keep the choice of regular or special schooling, and home-based education stays for severe and profound disabilities.

sections.title: What the data shows
sections.big_idea: Census, NSS, UDISE+ and ASER measure different things, so **triangulate** before you trust one number.
in_plain_words: UDISE+ 2025-26 shows 22.1 lakh children with special needs enrolled, which is 0.89% of total enrolment. Census 2011 put disability at 2.21% and the NSS 76th round at 2.2%. A school share below 1% means many disabled children are out of school, enrolled but unidentified, or both.

ASER 2024 shows 98.1% of children aged 6 to 14 enrolled, and only 23.4% of Std III children in government schools able to read a Std II text. National averages rise while groups stand still, so ask for tables by CWSN status. Some data does not exist at all, such as usable accessible toilets and teachers who sign.

diagram.note: then ask whether each missing child is out of school or unidentified

key_terms.meaning: The school census, with individual student records from 2022-23.
The 2018 survey of persons with disabilities.
Combine sources with different definitions to estimate a number.
A household test of reading and arithmetic in rural areas.
Breaking an average into groups, such as CWSN, ST and girls.

worked_example.title: The identification gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 10,000 school-age children in a block. Use the prevalence figures from the deck.
steps: Expected at 2.2% prevalence: 10,000 × 0.022 = 220 disabled children.
Identified at the UDISE+ share of 0.89%: 10,000 × 0.0089 = 89 children.
220 − 89 = 131 children missing from school records.
These are either out of school or unidentified; the two failures need different responses.
worked_example.answer: 131 children are missing from the records, to be found by a section 17(a) or door-to-door survey.

mistakes: Treating one source as the truth when two disagree. Check definitions and age bands first.
Celebrating a national average without a table by social group and CWSN status.
Reading ASER, a rural household survey, as a count of all children.

recall.q: What share of total enrolment are CWSN in UDISE+ 2025-26?
recall.a: 0.89%, or 22.1 lakh children.

recall.q: Which source is best for prevalence and schooling history?
recall.a: The NSS 76th round.

recall.q: What did ASER 2024 find for Std III reading?
recall.a: 23.4% of Std III children in government schools could read a Std II text.

recall.q: Why does inclusion start before Class 1?
recall.a: Only 10.1% of people with disability aged 3 to 35 ever had pre-school intervention, yet the years before six are when support changes the most.

sections.title: Neighbours' laws
sections.big_idea: Every South Asian state has ratified the CRPD, but **domestic laws differ** in how hard they push schools to change.
in_plain_words: All eight states are now parties to the CRPD, with Bhutan the last in March 2024. Ratification binds the country in international law, and how far it binds courts depends on each constitution. India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka have disability laws with education provisions of different strength.

Bangladesh defines inclusive, integrated and special education. Nepal puts Braille education and mother tongue schooling in its Constitution. Pakistan's 2020 Act applies only to Islamabad Capital Territory. Sri Lanka's 1996 Act bars discrimination in admission and says little more. None has followed General Comment 4 to a single system.

diagram.caption: ratification dates in the order the countries joined

key_terms.meaning: A state's formal consent to be bound by a treaty.
In Bangladesh, mainstream school with special arrangements.
Pakistan's law, limited to the Islamabad Capital Territory.
Nepal's constitutional article on basic, secondary and Braille education.
A country's own statutes, which differ from the treaty.

worked_example.title: Read one row of the table
worked_example.setup: Compare how four laws answer whether refusal of admission is barred.
steps: India: yes, section 16(i).
Bangladesh: yes, section 33, with a complaint to a committee that can direct admission.
Pakistan ICT: yes, section 9(4).
Nepal bars fees in 21(3) and discrimination in 21(5), a different route to a similar protection.
worked_example.answer: All four protect admission, by different routes. Cite the law of the country where you work.

mistakes: Citing the ICT Act as Pakistan's national law. Check the provincial law.
Treating Sri Lanka's 1996 Act as the whole picture. Check for newer law.
Assuming ratification changes classrooms by itself. It binds the state; schools change through law and budget.

recall.q: Which country was the last in South Asia to ratify the CRPD?
recall.a: Bhutan, on 13 March 2024.

recall.q: What three kinds of schooling does Bangladesh's 2013 Act define?
recall.a: Inclusive, integrated and special education.

recall.q: What does Article 31(5) of Nepal's Constitution protect?
recall.a: Every community's right to education in its mother tongue up to secondary level.

recall.q: How long did Sri Lanka take from signature to ratification?
recall.a: Nine years.

sections.title: Classroom practice
sections.big_idea: A good lesson plans for variety **at the start**, so that fewer children need a separate fix.
in_plain_words: Universal Design for Learning builds options into a lesson: several ways to engage, to receive information and to show learning. Differentiation then responds to children the teacher knows, varying content, process, product, environment and pace around one learning goal. The two work together.

Home language matters. NEP paragraph 4.11 sets the home language as the medium of instruction to at least Grade 5. Multilingual education builds a bridge from the home language to the school language. Assistive technology, individual education plans and exam accommodations complete the picture. Most of it needs planning time more than money.

key_terms.meaning: Universal Design for Learning, a CAST framework with three principles.
Varying content, process or product around one goal.
An individual education plan: goals, accommodations, support and review.
A person who writes a candidate's answers in an exam.
Teaching that bridges the home language and the school language.

worked_example.title: Count the UDL gain
worked_example.setup: Illustrative Class 4 lesson in rural Jharkhand with 38 children.
steps: Before UDL: six children finish the sums.
After UDL: twenty-nine children finish.
38 − 6 = 32 children did not finish before.
29 ÷ 38 = 0.76, so about 76% finished after the redesign.
worked_example.answer: From 6 of 38 to 29 of 38 finishing, with no new money. The change came from planning.

mistakes: Treating a quiet corner or extra time as a favour. They are accommodations the Act and the CRPD describe.
Letting differentiation harden into a permanent slow group that never meets the full content.
Buying a device with no training, repair or charging plan.

recall.q: What are the three UDL principles?
recall.a: Multiple means of engagement, of representation, and of action and expression.

recall.q: Which NEP paragraph sets the home language as the medium of instruction?
recall.a: Paragraph 4.11.

recall.q: What does RPwD section 16(iv) require?
recall.a: Necessary support, individualised or otherwise, in environments that maximise development.

recall.q: When should a school apply for exam accommodations?
recall.a: Early, with the certificate and records ready well before the Class 10 board registration deadline.

sections.title: Teachers and support staff
sections.big_idea: Inclusion depends on the **class teacher every day**, supported by specialists who visit.
in_plain_words: A special educator may visit a school once a week while the class teacher is present every day. Section 17 of the RPwD Act and NEP 6.14 both require teachers to be trained for diverse learners. Training alone is thin: teachers need time, a manageable class, accessible materials and a headteacher who backs accommodations.

Specialists fit into four support models: itinerant, resource room, co-teaching and cluster resource centre. Each trades reach against depth. Screening with PRASHAST flags a child for a closer look and diagnoses nothing. Families know how the child communicates. A district can plan staffing step by step from children to staff, training and equipment.

diagram.caption: support, from daily presence to scarce specialists

key_terms.meaning: One special educator visits many schools on a cycle.
Class teacher and special educator teach the class together.
NCERT's screening checklist and app for 21 disabilities.
Special educators must be registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India.
A contractual specialist, common under Samagra Shiksha.

worked_example.title: Plan the staff for a district
worked_example.setup: Illustrative district: 1,800 schools in 60 clusters, 3,600 CWSN enrolled.
steps: Today: 45 contractual resource persons, about 80 enrolled CWSN each.
45 × 80 = 3,600, which matches the enrolled count.
First-step target: one special educator per cluster, 60 posts.
1,800 ÷ 60 = 30 schools in each cluster for that educator to support.
worked_example.answer: 60 posts for 60 clusters, each covering 30 schools. Map each cost line to Samagra Shiksha and the state budget.

mistakes: Training teachers for three days and sending them back to a class of 60 with no follow-up.
Using a screening flag as a diagnosis. NCERT says PRASHAST is not for certification or labelling.
Hiring special educators without checking Rehabilitation Council registration.

recall.q: Why is the class teacher central to inclusion?
recall.a: The specialist visits weekly while the class teacher is present every day.

recall.q: What does NCERT warn about PRASHAST?
recall.a: It should not be used for certification or labelling.

recall.q: Name the four support models.
recall.a: Itinerant, resource room, co-teaching and cluster resource centre.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court hold on special teachers in 2021?
recall.a: They must be qualified and registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India.

sections.title: Measuring inclusion
sections.big_idea: Ask about **difficulty in specific activities**, and the counts stop depending on stigma and certificates.
in_plain_words: A question such as is this child disabled depends on stigma, certificates and the interviewer. The Washington Group Short Set asks six questions with four graded answers. The Child Functioning Module, finalised in 2016, covers children aged 2 to 17 and is answered by the caregiver. A Teacher Version and an Inclusive Education Module bring measurement into schools.

Impairment categories and functional difficulty answer different questions. Categories guide specialist services and certificate-linked entitlements; functional questions count children and compare them across places. You need both. A baseline runs in five steps, and a short set of indicators compares children with and without difficulty in the same schools.

right.title: Functional difficulty
items: Give no diagnosis and decide no entitlement

key_terms.meaning: Washington Group Short Set, six questions for adults.
Child Functioning Module, for children aged 2 to 4 and 5 to 17.
The teacher version, with 20 questions.
Inclusive Education Module on environmental factors.
The first measurement, used to judge change later.

worked_example.title: An out-of-school rate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a door-to-door CFM survey finds 400 children with functional difficulty aged 6 to 18, of whom 30 are out of school.
steps: Share out of school: 30 ÷ 400 = 0.075.
Per 1,000 children with difficulty: 0.075 × 1,000 = 75.
Compare with the rate for children without difficulty in the same villages.
The gap between the two rates is the measure of inclusion.
worked_example.answer: 75 per 1,000 children with difficulty are out of school. The comparison group gives it meaning.

mistakes: Treating a functional screen as a certificate, or a missing certificate as proof of no need.
Using the Short Set to count young children. It misses many developmental disabilities.
Collecting disability data on children without a lawful basis and a consent process.

recall.q: How many questions are in the Washington Group Short Set?
recall.a: Six.

recall.q: What are the four answer categories?
recall.a: No difficulty, some difficulty, a lot of difficulty, cannot do at all.

recall.q: Which age groups does the Child Functioning Module cover?
recall.a: Children aged 2 to 4 and 5 to 17.

recall.q: Which paragraph of General Comment 4 says accommodation may not depend on a medical diagnosis?
recall.a: Paragraph 30.

sections.title: A practitioner's toolkit
sections.big_idea: A three-part audit, a decision table and a worked year turn **law into weekly routine**.
in_plain_words: The school audit has three parts: the building, teaching and support, and records, families and governance. Walk the route a child would walk, observe a full lesson, and score each item from 0 to 3. Report scores by item, because a single total hides the item that keeps a child out.

The decision table pairs common situations with a first action and a legal basis. The worked example follows a block in Nandurbar for a year: find the children, fix the schools, support them, count the results. Finding children turned out cheaper than teaching them well. Six recurring mistakes close the section.

diagram.caption: the audit in the order you walk it

key_terms.meaning: 0 not in place, 1 on paper, 2 partly used, 3 used and checked.
A map from situation to first action and legal basis.
The step above the district for disability complaints.
The factor that limits progress next.
Set money aside so it cannot be spent elsewhere.

worked_example.title: Read the Nandurbar year
worked_example.setup: Illustrative block: door-to-door survey finds 260 children with difficulty, 70 of them out of school.
steps: At the end of the year 45 of the 70 are enrolled.
70 − 45 = 25 children still out of school.
260 − 70 = 190 children were in school at the start.
Attendance gap narrowed, reading gap unchanged: teaching is now the binding constraint.
worked_example.answer: 25 children remain out of school. The team's next budget goes to classroom support in place of more camps.

mistakes: Counting enrolment as success.
Spending most of the budget on camps and devices with no classroom change.
Running everything on contractual staff who leave when the project ends.

recall.q: How are audit items scored?
recall.a: 0 to 3: not in place, on paper only, partly used, used and checked in the last term.

recall.q: What is the first action when a private school refuses a disabled child under the 25% quota?
recall.a: A written complaint to the district education officer, with the refusal recorded.

recall.q: What did the Nandurbar example teach?
recall.a: Finding children is cheap compared with teaching them well, so budget year two for teacher support.

recall.q: What habit does the deck suggest for every review meeting?
recall.a: Ask which child the programme has not yet reached, and why.

notes.2: Twelve sections run in this order: meaning, models, who is left out, the RTE Act, the RPwD Act, NEP and Samagra Shiksha, data, neighbours' laws, classroom, staff, measurement, toolkit. If you work in a district office, **start with sections 5 and 12**. If you teach, start with sections 9 and 10.
notes.4: Read the definition as a sentence about **who must change**. The answer is the system. Notice the four things it lists: content, methods, structures and strategies. When you read a programme document later, ask which of the four it actually alters, because a ramp on its own changes only one of them.
notes.5: Learn the four words as a ladder: exclusion, segregation, integration, inclusion. What separates the last two is **who adjusts**. The deaf child at the back of Class 4 with no interpreter has been integrated, and no more. Use these four terms to classify any project before you praise it.
notes.6: Four clauses, four consequences. The clause to remember is (a): the right belongs to **the child**, so a parent's wish to keep a daughter at home does not end the state's duty. Clause (c) tells a finance officer that this spending is also poverty and employment policy. Quote the clause letter when you argue.
notes.7: Salamanca matters for one reversal. Separate provision stopped being the default and became **the exception that needs a reason**. Keep the cost-effectiveness line from paragraph 2 ready for finance ministries, because they often respond to an efficiency argument sooner than to a rights argument.
notes.8: Salamanca's list is wide: disabled and gifted children, working and street children, nomadic children, minority-language children and marginalised groups. Match each line to a child you know in your own district. This wide frame is the root of NEP 2020's term SEDG, which you meet in section 6.
notes.9: Article 24(2) is five clauses you can recite: no exclusion, local access, accommodation, support, individual measures. Pair each with an object. **Clause (c) is the ramp, the scribe and the extra time. Clause (e) is the individual plan.** India ratified on 1 October 2007.
notes.10: Article 24 reaches past admission to communication and staff. Clause 3 covers Braille, sign language and the most suitable modes. Clause 4 requires **teachers who can use them**, including teachers with disabilities. Check any plan for both halves: tools for the child and adults who can use them.
notes.11: Two paragraphs to underline. Paragraph 31 makes accommodation **owed now**, with no waiting for the budget. Paragraph 40 says two parallel systems cannot be sustained. Keep paragraph 40 in mind for slide 42, where India's own law offers families a choice of school.
notes.12: Read the three parity numbers as a slope: 0.91, 0.68, 0.34. The poorest nearly match the richest at primary and fall far behind by upper secondary. **Exclusion grows at every stage**, so ask what your programme does after Class 5, because stopping there finishes a third of the job.
notes.14: Listen for the model in what people say. A headteacher who calls a child unready for school is using the medical model. A district officer who asks why there is no ramp is using another. Disability certificates are medical-model tools, so **you will meet that model daily**.
notes.15: Walk the four boxes with any child you know: impairment, barrier, result, fix. The impairment stays the same and **the barrier moves**. Barriers can be listed, costed and removed, which is why planners like this model and why the audit in section 12 is built on it.
notes.16: The rights model adds three things: a duty bearer, a standard and a remedy. Section 2(s) defines disability as impairment **in interaction with barriers**, and section 3(1) gives the right to equality. In practice a refused admission becomes a legal wrong that a forum can hear.
notes.17: The ICF lets you describe a child by what she finds hard in class, with no diagnosis needed. That is why surveys ask about seeing, hearing, walking and remembering. Keep this idea for section 11: **functional questions find more children** than a yes or no question about disability.
notes.18: Use the table as a checklist. For any proposal, ask which column its money sits in. Real programmes mix all four, and that is normal. The warning sign is a plan that funds only identification. **A good proposal spends more on the classroom than on the label.**
notes.19: Follow the statute in documents, and ask families which words they prefer. The practical catch is benchmark disability: it needs 40% certified, so a child with a mild learning disability may miss entitlements such as free devices under section 17(g) while **still needing help in class**.
notes.20: Disability combines with gender, caste, language and place. The boy and girl gap is small, 62% against 60%. **The larger gaps lie between kinds of disability**: 54% of children with multiple disabilities never attended. Serving the easiest children first makes a programme look good and leaves these children where they were.
notes.22: Pakistan has the steepest slope: 65.9% against 14.6%, a ratio of about four and a half. India's ratio is about 1.4. The slide shows that **poverty alone excludes** before any other identity is added. Ask which wealth quintile your programme actually reaches.
notes.23: The number to hold is 1 in 10 children, from functional surveys. School records in South Asia show far fewer. The gap comes from definitions, so **a low count can hide a high need**. Notice also that children with difficulty communicating and caring for themselves are most likely to be out of school.
notes.24: Split the 27% who never attended from the 12% who attended and left. The second group were enrolled once, so **the barrier that pushed them out is often in the school itself**. Look for them first in any re-enrolment drive. Census 2011 is still the latest completed census.
notes.25: Two lessons from NSS 2018. Special schools reached only 4.1% of those outside ordinary school, so they are a small part of the picture. And only 10.1% had any pre-school intervention. **Use both numbers** when someone proposes that the answer is simply more special schools.
notes.26: Follow the disabled line down: 1.1% of primary enrolment, 0.25% at higher secondary, a fall of more than three quarters. SC and ST shares fall too, and girls fall further within each group. These are 2016-17 figures, so **check the latest UDISE+ tables** before quoting a current level.
notes.27: Read the table as a list of routes: fees, distance, language, safety, stigma, documents and migration timing. **Name the route before choosing the remedy.** Notice the legal wrinkle in row four: minority-run schools sit outside the RTE Act, and that ruling has been referred for reconsideration.
notes.28: Enrolment and attendance leave a gap: a child who cannot follow the teacher is excluded inside the room. The GEM paper recommends **six years of mother tongue instruction** and teachers trained to teach in two languages. Remember the headline figure, 40% of the global population without education in a language they understand.
notes.30: Learn the chain: Article 21A in 2002, then the RTE Act in force from 1 April 2010. The right covers Classes 1 to 8, ages six to fourteen. **Pre-school is a 'may' and secondary is outside the Act.** The 2014 Constitution Bench upheld the amendments.
notes.31: Section 3 gives every child a right to **a neighbourhood school**, and section 3(2) bars any fee that could stop a child finishing. Two definitions matter. Section 2(d), disadvantaged group, includes disabled children. Section 2(e), weaker section, is income-based. The 2012 amendment added disability.
notes.32: Here is a cross-reference trap. Section 3(3) points to the 1995 Act, which has been repealed. Read the RTE Act together with section 31 of the RPwD Act, which **overrides and extends it up to age eighteen**. Home-based education stays legal, so ask for the audit that NEP calls for.
notes.33: Follow the quota as five verbs: notify, apply, allot, study, reimburse. Disabled children fall within section 2(d), so they can use the 25% seats. Admission is only the start. Section 13 bars screening, so **a test at the gate is a breach**, and the fine can reach twenty-five thousand rupees.
notes.34: The counts rise from 16.76 to 21.58 to 32.67 lakh. They count seats and say nothing about the child's experience, such as hidden charges or being seated apart. For a disabled child the seat can become **integration without inclusion** if the school has no accessible toilet or trained teacher.
notes.35: Read the three rulings in order. In 2012 the Court upheld the Act for unaided non-minority schools. In 2014 it took minority schools outside it. In 2025 a bench doubted that view, and the reference is pending. Until then many schools serving poor children sit **outside the 25% quota**.
notes.36: Use the two Acts as a pair. Cite the RTE Act for the neighbourhood school and the ban on screening. Cite the RPwD Act for what happens inside the school and for free education to eighteen. A parent on the School Management Committee is **often the quickest route to a ramp**.
notes.38: Four numbers organise the Act: 21 specified disabilities, a 40% threshold, free education from 6 to 18, and 5% of higher education seats. Sections 16 to 18 cover every child **with or without a certificate**. Sections 31 and 32 need the certificate. Keep that split in mind whenever someone asks who is covered.
notes.39: Two definitions, two jobs. Section 2(m) describes the system and section 2(y) describes what one child is owed. Watch the phrase disproportionate or undue burden. General Comment 4 says a school **cannot use it to evade the duty**, so a refusal to provide a board-exam scribe is hard to defend.
notes.40: Eight duties become eight monitor questions in the right-hand column. Use them as a visit checklist. 'Shall endeavour' is softer than 'shall', yet clause (vii) gives you firm ground for data: **each disabled child's participation, progress and completion must be monitored**.
notes.41: Section 17 is the government's building plan. Chase two items first: (a), the survey every five years, and (g), free books and devices to eighteen. **Ask your district for its section 17(a) survey.** It is the baseline that every inclusion plan needs.
notes.42: Hold both arguments. Special schools gather sign language users and trained teachers, which many deaf families value. Yet General Comment 4 warns against permanent dual systems. A defensible stance for a practitioner is to **keep the choice open now and measure every year** whether ordinary schools can serve more of those children.
notes.43: Use the Schedule to widen your idea of who counts. It brings specific learning disabilities, autism, mental illness and blood disorders into the legal frame. A school may owe duties to children it **never thought of as disabled**. Read the right-hand column for the classroom question each group raises.
notes.44: This is a continuing case, followed state by state. Two points matter. The courts now treat regular, qualified posts as part of the right, and contractual staffing is fragile. Whether special teachers must also pass the TET is **still unresolved**, with about 4,900 vacant posts recorded in Uttar Pradesh.
notes.46: Memorise SEDG as five groups: gender, socio-cultural, geographical, disability and socio-economic identities. The frame is wide, which is also its risk, because everything becomes a priority. For each later paragraph, ask **which group it actually funds**.
notes.47: Four instruments: a Gender-Inclusion Fund, Special Education Zones, boarding and girls' schools, and a menu of what works by group. Match each to the barrier it removes: toilets and bicycles for distance and safety, boarding for far-off students. These are proposals, so **look for the matching budget line**.
notes.48: Paragraph 6.10 gives the inclusion of children with disabilities **the highest priority**. Paragraph 6.11 lists resources: cross-disability special educators, resource centres, barrier-free access, devices and ISL modules. Paragraph 6.12 keeps the choice of school and home-based education for severe cases.
notes.49: Two paragraphs ask for early identification and for teacher education on learning disabilities. The quotation at the foot is the one to remember: the measures are called essential and also short of enough, so **school culture itself must change**. Paragraph 6.20 adds curriculum bias to the list.
notes.50: Samagra Shiksha merged three schemes in 2018 and is the main central money for inclusion. Inclusive Education is one of **fifteen interventions**. The 2021 to 2026 period ended on 31 March 2026 and states are approving the next phase, so check which phase a plan quotes.
notes.51: Read the table as a shopping list: stipends, camps, resource centres, special educators and NIOS support. The 23,000 or so special educators supported each year is the figure to set beside the Supreme Court's supervision. **Ask where each line appears in your state's budget.**
notes.53: Use UDISE+ as your school-side baseline. Read the ramp figure carefully: 58.2% with ramps and handrails leaves 41.8% without. A ramp is **the starting point of accessibility**, since toilets, upper floors and playgrounds matter as much. Retention at 51.9% also needs disaggregating.
notes.54: Schools report 0.89% of enrolment as CWSN, while surveys put disability near 2.2%. Either children are out of school or **enrolled without being identified**. The two failures need different responses: an enrolment drive for the first, screening and support for the second.
notes.55: Use this table to pick the right source for the question. The Census gives district counts, NSS gives prevalence and schooling history, UDISE+ gives enrolment and facilities. When two sources disagree, **check definitions and age bands first** before deciding which one is wrong.
notes.56: An enrolment of 98.1% sits beside a second fact: only 23.4% of Std III children in government schools can read a Std II text. Inclusion covers participation and achievement as well as attendance. Methods that help children behind for any reason **also help undiagnosed learning disabilities**.
notes.57: The gains are small and real: secondary GER from 68.5% to 71.7%, retention from 47.2% to 51.9%. The release gives national averages only. Ask for tables by CWSN status, ST and girls, because **a national average can rise while the groups you serve stand still**.
notes.58: Start before Class 1. Pre-primary enrolment of three-year-olds is 77.4%, yet only about one in ten disabled people aged 3 to 35 ever had pre-school intervention. The anganwadi is **where delays could first be noticed**, so plan links from anganwadi to screening to the Block Resource Centre.
notes.59: List what official data cannot tell you, then plan to collect it: out-of-school disabled children by district, days attended, learning levels, usable toilets, teachers with ISL or Braille. Treat child disability data as **sensitive**, and settle consent and lawful basis before you collect.
notes.61: Use the table for two things: a regional picture and the law you cite. Every state is now a party, with Bhutan last in March 2024. Ratification binds a country in international law, and what domestic courts do depends on each constitution. Sri Lanka took **nine years** from signature to ratification.
notes.62: Bangladesh separates three kinds of schooling: inclusive, integrated and special. **Integrated** means mainstream school with special arrangements, a middle step. Section 33 is the practical clause: a head may not refuse admission solely because of disability, and a complaint can bring a direction to admit.
notes.63: Nepal writes rights into the Constitution: Braille education in 31(4) and mother tongue schooling to secondary level in 31(5). The 2017 Act adds a ban on admission fees and more than one means of learning. If you work in Nepal, cite **the constitutional article first**, then section 21.
notes.64: Pakistan's Article 25A covers ages five to sixteen. The 2020 Act applies only to the Islamabad Capital Territory, so treat it as a model and **check the provincial law** where you work. Section 9(3) keeps special institutions beside inclusive ones.
notes.65: Sri Lanka's 1996 Act has one short education provision, a ban on discrimination in admission. It predates the CRPD by a decade. Ratification in 2016 brings Article 24 into the reporting duties. Advocacy can cite both, but **check for newer law** before treating 1996 as the whole picture.
notes.66: Scan each row and ask which country pushes ordinary schools hardest. India and Bangladesh define inclusive education, while Pakistan only describes its aims. All four keep special or integrated tracks, so **none has reached the single system of paragraph 40**.
notes.68: UDL is three questions asked at planning time: what keeps learners engaged, how is information presented, how can they show what they know. The ramp analogy helps: options built in from the start serve the children you expected and those you did not. **Use the three principles as headings** on a lesson plan.
notes.69: Compare the two lessons. Before: board work and copying, and six of 38 children finish. After: string, hand spans, bilingual naming, large print and three ways to answer, and twenty-nine finish. **None of it needed new money.** It needed planning time, which is why UDL belongs in pre-service training.
notes.70: Keep one goal for the class and vary the route. Five things can vary: content, process, product, environment and pace. The failure to avoid is permanent tracking, the slow group that never sees the full content. **Regroup often** and check that every child reached the goal.
notes.71: Paragraph 4.11 makes the home language the medium of instruction to at least Grade 5 and preferably Grade 8. 'Wherever possible' is the escape clause. In a class with five home languages and one teacher, the practical answer on the next slide is **a bilingual bridge**.
notes.72: Read the four steps as a bridge from the home language: speak it, add oral second language, read in both, then teach subjects in both. Reading skills **transfer** once a child knows what reading is. Plan graded material, and teachers or assistants who speak the children's languages.
notes.73: Start with what the child and family already use, because the low-tech column is a real column. Match each need to its legal hook in the last column when you ask for funds. A device with no training, repair or power for charging **has cost money and changed nothing**.
notes.74: An IEP has six parts: who the child is, present levels, three to five goals, accommodations, support and review. Indian law has no term IEP, yet sections 16(iv) and 16(vii) ask for the same things. Write the goals **so that anyone can check them**.
notes.75: Study Anjali's plan for its goals. Each has a number and a date: 30 words a minute by the end of term, 50 signs. The accommodations are small and cheap. Notice that she stays in her own class throughout, which is exactly the definition in section 2(m).
notes.76: Board exams are where many disabled students leave school, so apply for extra time, a scribe or a language exemption **early**. Classroom climate matters equally. Peer tutoring, clear rules on teasing, a visual timetable and a buddy cost almost nothing and help children with autism, anxiety or hearing loss most.
notes.78: A special educator may visit weekly, while the class teacher is there every day. So inclusion rests on a class teacher who has skills **and** time, support, materials and a backing headteacher. A three-day workshop followed by a class of 60 usually fades, so budget follow-up classroom visits.
notes.79: Know who does what: special educator, contractual resource person, therapist, interpreter and counsellor. The firm rule is that special educators must be registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India. Interpreters and in-school therapists are rare, so **check registration** whenever a programme hires.
notes.80: Four support models, each with a trade-off. Ask the same question of all four: does it change the ordinary classroom, or only remove the child for a while? **Co-teaching changes the class**, though it needs time and staff. Most districts mix models, and the table ranks none of them.
notes.81: PRASHAST screens for the 21 disabilities in the Act. NCERT's own warning is the line to remember: do not use it for certification or labelling. A flag means look closer. Budget for **what happens after the flag**, or screening raises hopes with no service behind it.
notes.82: Families know how the child communicates and what calms her. Invite them to draft the who-the-child-is part of the IEP. Avoid jargon, and avoid reading refusal of home-based education as lack of cooperation. NEP says educating disabled children is **the responsibility of the State**.
notes.83: Follow the method in the table: start from children, then staff, training, equipment and budget lines. The numbers are invented. The 45 resource persons spread over 3,600 enrolled children show how thin the cover is at about 80 children each, so **trace every line to a budget head**.
notes.85: Two requirements ask for counts: SDG 4.5.1 wants parity by disability status, and section 16(vii) wants every child monitored. The obstacle is the yes or no question. **Functional questions with graded answers** reduce the effect of stigma and certificates on the count.
notes.86: Six questions, four answers: no difficulty, some, a lot, cannot do at all. The graded scale lets you set and report a severity threshold. Remember the limit: the Short Set misses children under five and many developmental disabilities, which is **why the Child Functioning Module exists**.
notes.87: The CFM has two versions, ages 2 to 4 and 5 to 17, both answered by the caregiver. Remember the six shared areas and the extra ones for each age. The **emotion items** matter for schools: a child very anxious every day may hold no certificate and still need accommodation.
notes.88: Two newer tools bring measurement into schools. The teacher version has 20 questions and suits an EMIS. The Inclusive Education Module asks about the school environment for all children. For India, **the teacher version is the closest fit to UDISE+**, so pilot it in a few districts beside the CWSN categories.
notes.89: Use both columns. Categories tell you which specialist or device to plan and which entitlement needs a certificate. Functional questions tell you how many children face difficulty. **Never use a screen as a certificate**, and never read a missing certificate as proof that a child needs nothing.
notes.90: Five steps: adapt, sample, ask, link, report. People skip the link step, which joins children to school records and learning tests and gives you gaps by difficulty, sex and social group. Read the answer options aloud every time, and keep functional data apart from names in the analysis file.
notes.91: Six indicators, each with a data source. The principle at the end is the one to keep: **compare children with and without difficulty in the same schools**. That gap is the measure of inclusion. Pick one indicator per dimension before you collect anything.
notes.93: Walk the route a child would walk, at the hour she would walk it. The audit asks whether a ramp works, which no national dataset records. A ramp that ends at a step, or a toilet used as a store room, **shows up only on the walk**.
notes.94: Score part 2 only after you have observed a full lesson and talked to three children. Teachers' answers about their own practice are useful and incomplete. The question most worth asking is **what the last specialist visit changed**.
notes.95: Part 3 covers records, families and governance. Score each item from 0 to 3 and report scores by item. A single total **hides the item that keeps a child out**. Check one item first: whether there is a written way to complain about a refused admission.
notes.96: Use the table when a family comes to you. Pick the matching row, take the first action, and cite the legal basis. Escalate in steps: school, block, district, then the State Commissioner or the courts. **Keep copies of every letter.**
notes.97: Follow the block through four steps: find, fix the schools, support, count. After a year, 45 of the 70 out-of-school children are enrolled but the reading gap is unchanged. The lesson is that **finding children is cheap and teaching them well is the harder part**. Budget year two for classroom support.
notes.98: Six mistakes, each with a counter. Keep one on a sticky note: counting enrolment as success. Pair it with the closing habit, which is to ask at every review meeting **which child the programme has not yet reached, and why**.
notes.99: These are your next courses. Start with the three-part audit on one school you know, then read Disability Inclusion 101 for the wider rights picture. Survey Design 101 and the Data Protection course serve the baseline work in section 11, so **take them before you run a CFM survey**.
